transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-13
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Ibanez (Redwood SE), Jun Park (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (CTO, NimbusGrid), Leo Park (Platform Engineer), Marta Silva (Data Privacy), Ivan Korchev (SRE), Sam Bennett (ML Engineer)

Summary (auto):
High-level discovery for integrating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Focus on SDK adapter patterns (LangChain & LlamaIndex), gateway/proxy topology for on-prem requests, quota and rate-limiting expectations, and observability hooks (trace/span correlation, per-model metrics). Customer wants to validate throughput for mixed short/long context workloads and confirm data residency/KMS controls.

Topics:
- Integration patterns: direct SDK, proxy/gateway sidecar, LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors
- Rate limits, quotas, burst handling, dedicated capacity sizing
- Observability: tracing, token-level cost, model-level metrics, export hooks
- Security: VPC, SSO, KMS, audit logs

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sophie Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, um i'll kick off -- i'm sophie, i'm the AE on this account, and then marcus and jun are gonna cover the deep integration stuff.
[00:12] Aisha Rahman: thanks sophie, appreciate it. we wanted to get alignment on whether we go hosted or dedicated, and how messy the integration will be. we run a hybrid infra so data residency and vpc egress is a big thing.
[00:25] Marcus Ibanez: great, thanks aisha. quick note from our side: we see a lot of customers do a hybrid where the control plane is hosted but inference runs on dedicated pools or private. for NimbusGrid, given the residency note, private or dedicated are both candidates.
[00:39] Leo Park: yeah we can't have model inputs leaving our VPC for regulated traffic. is that the private offering that keeps everything on prem?
[00:48] Jun Park: right, the Private deployment is the one where the control plane can be customer managed and inference is inside your VPC or on-prem. there's an optional on-prem package if you need air-gap.
[00:58] Marta Silva: do you have SOC2 or ISO reports for that? and how does KMS integrate? we have to show encryption at rest with our KMS and proof of key separation.
[01:10] Marcus Ibanez: yes, we have SOC 2 reports; for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. the key material never leaves the HSM. i can attach the security pack after the call.
[01:20] Ivan Korchev: on throughput, our workload is weird: 60% short queries (1-50 tokens), 40% context-heavy retrieval-augmented requests up to 8k tokens. p95 latency target is around 300ms for short queries, and for the big ones we're ok with about 3s.
[01:35] Sophie Chen: that's helpful. on dedicated side we can size GPU pools and give an SLA for p95. for hosted it'd depend on model selection and we often recommend smaller models or aggressively cached prefixes for high qps short queries.
[01:47] Sam Bennett: can you describe the recommended gateway pattern? we have a Kong-based edge and want a proxy that handles token-level routing, rate limit enforcement, and optionally local KV cache to cut calls to the model.
[02:00] Marcus Ibanez: common pattern: client -> edge proxy (kong) -> request router service -> Redwood SDK or sidecar proxy. two flavors: 1) SDK-first: your app calls Redwood SDK directly with credentials and route/pinning, 2) proxy-first: you run a lightweight sidecar proxy (we provide a reference) that does routing, batching, kv cache and then forwards to Redwood. sidecar helps centralize quotas and observability.
[02:20] Leo Park: is that sidecar something we deploy on k8s as a daemonset?
[02:25] Jun Park: yes most customers deploy it as a k8s DaemonSet or as a per-pod sidecar. it's 0.5-1 vCPU and a little memory; it also exposes Prometheus metrics and an OpenTelemetry span out.
[02:37] Leo Park: nice — we need the Prom hooks. what about langchain / llamaindex? our ML codebase uses LangChain heavily.
[02:45] Marcus Ibanez: we have first-class adapters for LangChain and sample connector for LlamaIndex. i'll share the gist after this but the approach is simple: you plug in the Redwood client endpoint and we support streaming and function-calls semantics that LangChain expects. sometimes names get mismatched in transcripts — 'LlamaIndex' can be spelled 'Lama Index' but we support the connector.
[03:04] Aisha Rahman: streaming is critical for UX. are there quotas per second we need to be aware of? we expect bursty traffic after user events.
[03:14] Marcus Ibanez: on hosted it's a shared pool with soft rate limits; we enforce per-api key qps and token quotas to protect fairness. Dedicated gives you reserved throughput and you can configure burst buckets. Private you control it entirely. for burst handling we provide automated fallback to a cheaper model or queueing policy.
[03:32] Ivan Korchev: can fallback keep latency under threshold? for certain flows we need deterministic responses; queueing isn't acceptable.
[03:40] Jun Park: you can do multi-tier routing: primary high-perf model, secondary compatible but cheaper model for degraded quality but low latency. or you can route to a local cache if the prefix is hot. queueing is only for best-effort async jobs.
[03:54] Marta Silva: audit logs — do you give token-level logs? we can only allow logging of derived metadata, not raw PII.
[04:03] Marcus Ibanez: we provide configurable audit logs. customers can mask PII, disable full transcript retention, or keep meta-only. for Private, logs can stay in your storage.
[04:12] Sophie Chen: quick check — are there specific compliance docs you want now? we can share SOC2, ISO summary, and a KMS integration guide.
[04:20] Marta Silva: please send SOC2 and KMS integration guide. also need data residency statement.
[04:26] Sophie Chen: will do.
[04:29] [short pause / rustling papers]
[04:45] Leo Park: let's talk observability: we need per-route latency, token breakdown, model-level error rates, and traces that correlate with our request ids. how does Redwood export traces and metrics?
[04:58] Jun Park: we emit Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry spans, and we accept incoming trace context so you get end-to-end correlation. we also provide token-level cost breakdowns in the Console and an export API for usage.
[05:10] Ivan Korchev: is there a way to push metrics into our datadog/tempo pipeline?
[05:15] Marcus Ibanez: yes Prom remote write and OTLP exporters are supported, and many customers ship to Datadog, Tempo, New Relic.
[05:24] Sam Bennett: on SDK side: do you have a node + python client? we use python for ML and node for product.
[05:30] Jun Park: we have official SDKs: python, node, and a lightweight go client. all support streaming and function-like calls; the python client has a LangChain integration package.
[05:40] Sam Bennett: any quirks with the python SDK when used inside uvicorn/fastapi async apps?
[05:45] Marcus Ibanez: we've seen people use both sync and async; we provide async client patterns that are uvicorn friendly. one caveat: you must ensure the KV cache is shared or use the sidecar for consistent caching.
[05:56] Aisha Rahman: pricing — can you ballpark Dedicated vs Hosted for our expected qps? we might do a pilot with 100 qps sustained, spike to 500 qps for short windows.
[06:07] Sophie Chen: sure we can do that. high-level: hosted is pay-as-you-go and is easiest to start but cost per token is higher. Dedicated is commit-based with lower per-token cost and predictable latency; you'd pick a Dedicated pool sized for your sustained 100 qps with burst headroom. i'll follow up with a model and GPU sizing sketch.
[06:23] Leo Park: any minimum commitment for Dedicated?
[06:27] Sophie Chen: typical commitments are monthly or annual; we can structure a short pilot with a month trial and convert.
[06:33] Marcus Ibanez: for the architecture part, do you want us to show a sample sidecar helm chart in the deep-dive?
[06:39] Ivan Korchev: yes, helm chart and also expected metrics with dashboards are useful.
[06:44] Marcus Ibanez: noted. we'll bring a sample helm chart, Prom queries, and a LangChain example.
[06:51] [timestamp jump - mid call detailed discussion]
[16:05] Sam Bennett: walking through a sample request flow: user -> product server -> langchain agent -> retrieval -> call model. where do you recommend injecting the Redwood client?
[16:15] Jun Park: two options: 1) agent calls directly to Redwood SDK at the agent level, or 2) agent calls internal API which talks to sidecar. option 1 is lower latency but harder to centralize quotas; option 2 centralizes routing, caching, and observability. most infra teams pick option 2.
[16:30] Sam Bennett: how much overhead does sidecar add to small requests?
[16:34] Marcus Ibanez: we typically see an extra 10-30ms on the hot path, but you get caching and batching which often reduces p95 overall for high qps workloads.
[16:43] Leo Park: what about batching? our short queries could be batched; is that automatic?
[16:48] Jun Park: sidecar and server runtimes can do continuous batching. you set batch windows and token limits. for low latency customers we use very small windows and aggressive batching heuristics so latency stays within target.
[17:00] Aisha Rahman: i want to flag one constraint: legal wants that any export of logs to third party tooling must be under our control and be auditabled. can logs be disabled?
[17:10] Marcus Ibanez: yes, you can disable export and use a push model where your pipeline pulls masked metrics only. Private keeps logs in your environment entirely.
[17:18] Marta Silva: okay good.
[17:20] [brief cross talk about onboarding docs]
[17:35] Sophie Chen: quick demo ask — would you like a quick hosted-friendly demo to show latency and streaming, or shall we go straight to a technical deep dive?
[17:44] Aisha Rahman: let's do the deep dive next week with Ivan and Leo, demo for execs after.
[17:52] Sophie Chen: perfect. we'll schedule those.
[17:56] [noise; someone typing]
[18:10] Leo Park: one more: model versions and rollouts — can we pin a model per route and do canary rollouts? our ML team likes to experiment.
[18:19] Jun Park: yes, we support model pinning, A/B and canary rollouts; you can also configure automatic fallback to previous version if regressions detected.
[18:28] Sam Bennett: how do you handle long-running KV caches for retrieval augmented generation? if the model has a large kv cache and requests land on different pods, do you manage consistency?
[18:40] Marcus Ibanez: good question — our runtime supports distributed KV cache backends and sticky sessioning for tokens. sidecar can manage local cache with a TTL and we have options to use a shared Redis/managed cache for strong consistency.
[18:53] Ivan Korchev: can we run the Redis inside our VPC?
[18:56] Jun Park: absolutely. for Private/Dedicated we'd recommend hosting Redis in your VPC.
[19:02] [wrap-up segment]
[19:10] Sophie Chen: recap: we'll send SOC2 and KMS docs, Marcus will share LangChain/LlamaIndex examples and a sidecar helm chart, and Sophie will send Dedicated pricing sketch. we'll set up a technical deep-dive next week focused on helm chart, observability dashboards, and a small load-run to validate 100 qps.
[19:25] Aisha Rahman: perfect. can you also include a short checklist for security approvals?
[19:30] Marta Silva: yes that's helpful.
[19:33] Sophie Chen: will do. any final questions?
[19:36] Leo Park: no, thanks everyone.
[19:38] Ivan Korchev: thanks.
[19:40] Marcus Ibanez: thanks all, talk soon.
